title: Faker targets second Asian Games gold with Korea esports team
summary: Faker targets second Asian Games gold with Korea esports team  Korea JoongAng Daily
content:
Korea's 44-member esports team is aiming for five gold medals in Japan, with Faker returning for League of Legends.

The Korean national team for the esports category in the upcoming Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games held a kickoff ceremony Tuesday and shared their ambitions.

After debuting as a demonstration sport at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta, esports will be held as an official medal sport for the second time at the quadrennial event, set to kick off Sept. 19 in Japan this year.

Korea will send a team of 44 people, including 36 athletes, to compete in nine of 11 esports genres. The number of athletes and competing events has more than doubled from the 2022 Asian Games held in Hangzhou, China, the Korea esports Association said.

The esports star Lee Sang-hyeok, best known as Faker, will be vying for a second gold medal in League of Legends (LoL) as part of the national team this year.

"Since the Korean people have high hopes for the esports category, I want to fulfill that hope [...] and give them back pride and honor," Faker said at a press conference in Seoul, adding that he feels more excited than stressed ahead of the competition.

title: Has Fearless Draft actually improved champion diversity in League of Legends?
summary: Has Fearless Draft actually improved champion diversity in League of Legends?  Esports Insider
content:
Hajrudin Krdzic is a gaming and esports writer with over five years of experience covering live-service updates and competitive scenes. His first love was RTS games, which naturally grew into a long-term passion for MOBAs like League of Legends. He has also occasionally dipped into tactical shooters like Counter-Strike 2, roguelikes like Hades, and hero shooters such as Overwatch and Marvel Rivals.

Chadley Kemp (preferably just "Chad") has nearly a decade of editorial experience spanning esports, gaming, crypto, and betting content, covering everything from Counter-Strike and VALORANT to League of Legends and Dota 2. Outside of esports, Chadley holds a Ph.D. in Physiology and has published research in several peer-reviewed scientific journals.

TheLeague of Legendspro circuit used to have a drafting problem, but hasFearless Draftactually changed that?

In the past, you could finish game 1 of a best-of-five, load into game 2, and see half of the same champions again. Maybe they swapped sides or banned a priority pick, but more often than not, you are basically watching another version of the same draft.

Even at Worlds, things could get stale by the time we reached the knockout stage. Teams end up handshaking drafts, and suddenly, we’re watching the same boringCorkivs.Azirmatchup in mid lane over and over again. Fearless Draft was supposed to change that.

On paper, the format inevitably creates variety. If a best-of-five series reaches game 5, 40 champions have already been removed through the previous picks before the regular bans even begin. But that raises a more interesting question:
